description:
fz-5xp.14 asked for Elixir's two small self-owned tables in fz source, in their
own module so demand-driven per-module loading pays for them. The whitespace
table (25 codepoints) landed that way. CASE MAPPING did not.

MEASURED: 1,357 non-ASCII simple upcase pairs and 1,366 downcase, so 2,723
clauses. As fz clauses they go through the DISPATCH MATRIX, which makes compile
work proportional to the TABLE rather than to the program -- the opposite of
what fz is for, and the sort of thing the census pins exist to catch.

The fz-native alternative that avoids the clause count is a sorted table encoded
as a literal BINARY, binary-searched. That keeps one clause, but every lookup
allocates a stub for the literal, so it is one allocation per character cased.

So it is a runtime primitive: fz_binary_upcase / fz_binary_downcase over Rust's
char tables. FULL casing, matching Elixir's default mode, so "straße" upcases
to "STRASSE".

THE TICKET'S DESIGN GOAL SURVIVES THE MOVE, which is why this is a placement
decision rather than a loss. It asked for ONE coherent Unicode version, and the
reason it could ask is that Elixir cannot have one: its case mapping is Unicode
17 while OTP's grapheme breaking is Unicode 16. Rust's char tables are one
version, and when fz owns grapheme breaking (the next_grapheme_size/1 seam) it
will be the same one.

DONE = the table is fz data rather than either fz clauses or Rust. That needs
one of: a literal that can be read without allocating per lookup, or a table
representation the dispatch matrix does not expand.
title: The Unicode case table lives in the runtime because 2,723 fz clauses would not be proportional
